title: Social categorization and similarity in intergroup behaviour

source.title: Social categorization and similarity in intergroup behaviour

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Is simply naming groups enough to produce favoritism, or do people also need to think group members are similar?

fields.label: What the paper covers
fields.value: One 2×2 experiment contrasts explicit categorization and perceived similarity, with reward allocations as behavior.

fields.label: Across the paper
fields.value: Explicit group labels were sufficient for own-group favoritism in this task. Perceived similarity had a weaker influence, and fairness still mattered.

fields.label: Expectation or comparison
fields.value: The design separates the prediction that a group label alone can produce favoritism from the claim that perceived similarity is necessary.

fields.label: Interpretation and limits
fields.value: The sample was 75 boys from one school. The four sessions corresponded to the four conditions, so the design does not separately estimate session and condition effects.
fields.derivation: Scope of the published evidence and, where linked, differences from the Bench adaptation.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Seventy-five boys aged 14–16 allocated rewards using matrices. The four conditions crossed being told about explicit groups with apparent similarity on prior preferences. The matrices distinguish own-group favoritism, fairness and total joint reward.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: Explicit categorization produced favoritism even when group membership was known to be arbitrary. Similarity also contributed, but more weakly. Fairness remained evident across conditions.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Compare matrix pull scores within and between conditions and analyze a combined favoritism score. Some choices pit favoritism against maximum joint payoff or fairness.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: Both categorization conditions showed a significant pull toward own-group favoritism in the Figure 1 comparison. The authors treat the similarity result for maximum joint payoff as uncertain.
